L24: # ReOpenFile function (winbase.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Reopens the specified file system object with different access rights, sharing mode, and flags.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `HANDLE ReOpenFile(
L37:       [in] HANDLE hOriginalFile,
L38:       [in] DWORD  dwDesiredAccess,
L39:       [in] DWORD  dwShareMode,
L40:       [in] DWORD  dwFlagsAndAttributes
L41:     );
L42:     `
L43: ## Parameters
L44: 
L45: `[in] hOriginalFile`
L46: 
L47: A handle to the object to be reopened. The object must have been created by the 【5†CreateFile】 function.
L48: 
L49: `[in] dwDesiredAccess`
L50: 
L51: The required access to the object. For a list of values, see 【6†File Security and Access Rights】. You cannot request an access mode that conflicts with the sharing mode specified in a previous open request whose handle is still open.
L52: If this parameter is zero (0), the application can query device attributes without accessing the device. This is useful if an application wants to determine the size of a floppy disk drive and the formats it supports without requiring a floppy in the drive.
L53: 
L54: `[in] dwShareMode`
L55: 
L56: The sharing mode of the object. You cannot request a sharing mode that conflicts with the access mode specified in a previous open request whose handle is still open.
L57: If this parameter is zero (0) and 【5†CreateFile】 succeeds, the object cannot be shared and cannot be opened again until the handle is closed.
L58: 
L59: To enable other processes to share the object while your process has it open, use a combination of one or more of the following values to specify the type of access they can request when they open the object. These sharing options remain in effect until you close the handle to the object.
L60: 
L61: Value  | Meaning
L62: --- | ---
L63: FILE_SHARE_DELETE
L64: 0x00000004
L65:  | Enables subsequent open operations on the object to request delete access. Otherwise, other processes cannot open the object if they request delete access. If the object has already been opened with delete access, the sharing mode must include this flag.
L66: FILE_SHARE_READ
L67: 0x00000001
L68:  | Enables subsequent open operations on the object to request read access. Otherwise, other processes cannot open the object if they request read access. If the object has already been opened with read access, the sharing mode must include this flag.
L69: FILE_SHARE_WRITE
L70: 0x00000002
L71:  | Enables subsequent open operations on the object to request write access. Otherwise, other processes cannot open the object if they request write access. If the object has already been opened with write access, the sharing mode must include this flag.
L72: 
L73: `[in] dwFlagsAndAttributes`
L74: 
L75: The file flags. This parameter can be one or more of the following values.
L76: 
L77: Value  | Meaning
L78: --- | ---
L79: FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS
L80: 0x02000000
L81:  | Indicates that the file is being opened or created for a backup or restore operation. The system ensures that the calling process overrides file security checks, provided it has the SE_BACKUP_NAME and SE_RESTORE_NAME privileges. For more information, see 【7†Changing Privileges in a Token】. You can also set this flag to obtain a handle to a directory. Where indicated, a directory handle can be passed to some functions in place of a file handle.
L82: FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE
L83: 0x04000000
L84:  | Indicates that the operating system is to delete the file immediately after all of its handles have been closed, not just the specified handle but also any other open or duplicated handles. Subsequent open requests for the file fail, unless FILE_SHARE_DELETE is used.
L85: FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING
L86: 0x20000000
L87:  | Instructs the system to open the file with no intermediate buffering or caching. When combined with FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, the flag gives maximum asynchronous performance, because the I/O does not rely on the synchronous operations of the memory manager. However, some I/O operations take longer, because data is not being held in the cache. An application must meet specific requirements when working with files opened with FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING:
L88:   * File access must begin at byte offsets within the file that are integer multiples of the volume sector size.
L89:   * File access must be for numbers of bytes that are integer multiples of the volume sector size. For example, if the sector size is 512 bytes, an application can request reads and writes of 512, 1024, 1536, or 2048 bytes, but not of 335, 981, or 7171 bytes.
L90:   * Buffer addresses for read and write operations should be sector aligned (aligned on addresses in memory that are integer multiples of the volume sector size). Depending on the disk, this requirement may not be enforced.
L91: One way to align buffers on integer multiples of the volume sector size is to use 【8†VirtualAlloc】 to allocate the buffers. It allocates memory that is aligned on addresses that are integer multiples of the operating system memory page size. Because both memory page and volume sector sizes are powers of 2, this memory is also aligned on addresses that are integer multiples of a volume sector size.
L92: Memory pages are 4-8 KB in size; sectors are 512 bytes (hard disks) or 2048 bytes (CD), and therefore, volume sectors can never be larger than memory pages. An application can determine a volume sector size by calling the 【9†GetDiskFreeSpace】 function.
L93: FILE_FLAG_OPEN_NO_RECALL
L94: 0x00100000
L95:  | Indicates that the file data is requested, but it should continue to reside in remote storage. It should not be transported back to local storage. This flag is intended for use by remote storage systems.
L96: FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT
L97: 0x00200000
L98:  | When this flag is used, normal 【10†reparse point】 processing does not occur, and ReOpenFile attempts to open the reparse point. When a file is opened, a file handle is returned, whether or not the filter that controls the reparse point is operational. This flag cannot be used with the CREATE_ALWAYS flag. If the file is not a reparse point, then this flag is ignored.
L99: FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED
L100: 0x40000000
L101:  | Instructs the system to initialize the object, so that operations that take a significant amount of time to process return ERROR_IO_PENDING. When the operation is finished, the specified event is set to the signaled state. When you specify FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, the file read and write functions must specify an 【11†OVERLAPPED】 structure. That is, when FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED is specified, an application must perform overlapped reading and writing.

L24: # GetSecurityInfo function (aclapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: The GetSecurityInfo function retrieves a copy of the 【5†security descriptor】 for an object specified by a handle.
L33: ## Syntax
L34: 
L35:     `DWORD GetSecurityInfo(
L36:       [in]            HANDLE               handle,
L37:       [in]            SE_OBJECT_TYPE       ObjectType,
L38:       [in]            SECURITY_INFORMATION SecurityInfo,
L39:       [out, optional] PSID                 *ppsidOwner,
L40:       [out, optional] PSID                 *ppsidGroup,
L41:       [out, optional] PACL                 *ppDacl,
L42:       [out, optional] PACL                 *ppSacl,
L43:       [out, optional] PSECURITY_DESCRIPTOR *ppSecurityDescriptor
L44:     );
L45:     `
L46: ## Parameters
L47: 
L48: `[in] handle`
L49: 
L50: A handle to the object from which to retrieve security information.
L51: 
L52: `[in] ObjectType`
L53: 
L54: 【6†SE_OBJECT_TYPE】 enumeration value that indicates the type of object.
L55: 
L56: `[in] SecurityInfo`
L57: 
L58: A set of bit flags that indicate the type of security information to retrieve. This parameter can be a combination of the 【7†SECURITY_INFORMATION】 bit flags.
L59: 
L60: `[out, optional] ppsidOwner`
L61: A pointer to a variable that receives a pointer to the owner SID in the security descriptor returned in ppSecurityDescriptor. The returned pointer is valid only if you set the OWNER_SECURITY_INFORMATION flag. This parameter can be NULL if you do not need the owner SID.
L62: 
L63: `[out, optional] ppsidGroup`
L64: A pointer to a variable that receives a pointer to the primary group SID in the returned 【5†security descriptor】. The returned pointer is valid only if you set the GROUP_SECURITY_INFORMATION flag. This parameter can be NULL if you do not need the group SID.
L65: 
L66: `[out, optional] ppDacl`
L67: A pointer to a variable that receives a pointer to the DACL in the returned security descriptor. The returned pointer is valid only if you set the DACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION flag. This parameter can be NULL if you do not need the DACL.
L68: 
L69: `[out, optional] ppSacl`
L70: 
L71: A pointer to a variable that receives a pointer to the SACL in the returned security descriptor. The returned pointer is valid only if you set the SACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION flag. This parameter can be NULL if you do not need the SACL.
L72: `[out, optional] ppSecurityDescriptor`
L73: 
L74: A pointer to a variable that receives a pointer to the security descriptor of the object. When you have finished using the pointer, free the returned buffer by calling the 【8†LocalFree】 function.
L75: 
L76: This parameter is required if any one of the ppsidOwner, ppsidGroup, ppDacl, or ppSacl parameters is not NULL.
L77: ## Return value
L78: 
L79: If the function succeeds, the return value is ERROR_SUCCESS.
L80: 
L81: If the function fails, the return value is a nonzero error code defined in WinError.h.
L82: ## Remarks
L83: 
L84: If the ppsidOwner, ppsidGroup, ppDacl, and ppSacl parameters are non-NULL, and the SecurityInfo parameter specifies that they be retrieved from the object, those parameters will point to the corresponding parameters in the security descriptor returned in ppSecurityDescriptor.
L85: To read the owner, group, or DACL from the object's security descriptor, the calling process must have been granted READ_CONTROL access when the handle was opened. To get READ_CONTROL access, the caller must be the owner of the object or the object's DACL must grant the access.
L86: To read the SACL from the security descriptor, the calling process must have been granted ACCESS_SYSTEM_SECURITY access when the handle was opened. The proper way to get this access is to enable the SE_SECURITY_NAME privilege in the caller's current token, open the handle for ACCESS_SYSTEM_SECURITY access, and then disable the privilege. For information about the security implications of enabling privileges, see 【9†Running with Special Privileges】.
L87: You can use the GetSecurityInfo function with the following types of objects:
L88:   * Local or remote files or directories on an NTFS file system
L89:   * Named pipes
L90:   * Local or remote printers
L91:   * Local or remote Windows services
L92:   * Network shares
L93:   * Registry keys
L94:   * Semaphores, events, mutexes, and waitable timers
L95:   * Processes, threads, jobs, and file-mapping objects
L96:   * Interactive service window stations and desktops
L97:   * Directory service objects
L98: This function does not handle race conditions. If your thread calls this function at the approximate time that another thread changes the object's security descriptor, then this function could fail.
L99: #### Examples
L100: 
L101: For an example that uses this function, see 【10†Finding the Owner of a File Object】.
L102:

L24: # SetSecurityInfo function (aclapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: The SetSecurityInfo function sets specified security information in the 【5†security descriptor】 of a specified object. The caller identifies the object by a handle.
L33: 
L34: To set the SACL of an object, the caller must have the SE_SECURITY_NAME privilege enabled.
L35: ## Syntax
L36: 
L37:     `DWORD SetSecurityInfo(
L38:       [in]           HANDLE               handle,
L39:       [in]           SE_OBJECT_TYPE       ObjectType,
L40:       [in]           SECURITY_INFORMATION SecurityInfo,
L41:       [in, optional] PSID                 psidOwner,
L42:       [in, optional] PSID                 psidGroup,
L43:       [in, optional] PACL                 pDacl,
L44:       [in, optional] PACL                 pSacl
L45:     );
L46:     `
L47: ## Parameters
L48: 
L49: `[in] handle`
L50: 
L51: A handle to the object for which to set security information.
L52: 
L53: `[in] ObjectType`
L54: 
L55: A member of the 【6†SE_OBJECT_TYPE】 enumeration that indicates the type of object identified by the handle parameter.
L56: 
L57: `[in] SecurityInfo`
L58: 
L59: A set of bit flags that indicate the type of security information to set. This parameter can be a combination of the 【7†SECURITY_INFORMATION】 bit flags.
L60: 
L61: `[in, optional] psidOwner`
L62: A pointer to a SID that identifies the owner of the object. The SID must be one that can be assigned as the owner SID of a security descriptor. The SecurityInfo parameter must include the OWNER_SECURITY_INFORMATION flag. This parameter can be NULL if you are not setting the owner SID.
L63: 
L64: `[in, optional] psidGroup`
L65: A pointer to a SID that identifies the primary group of the object. The SecurityInfo parameter must include the GROUP_SECURITY_INFORMATION flag. This parameter can be NULL if you are not setting the primary group SID.
L66: 
L67: `[in, optional] pDacl`
L68: A pointer to the new DACL for the object. This parameter is ignored unless the value of the SecurityInfo parameter includes the DACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION flag. If the value of the SecurityInfo parameter includes the DACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION flag and the value of this parameter is set to NULL, full access to the object is granted to everyone. For information about null DACLs, see 【8†Creating a DACL】.
L69: 
L70: `[in, optional] pSacl`
L71: A pointer to the new SACL for the object. The SecurityInfo parameter must include any of the following flags: SACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION, LABEL_SECURITY_INFORMATION, ATTRIBUTE_SECURITY_INFORMATION, SCOPE_SECURITY_INFORMATION, or BACKUP_SECURITY_INFORMATION. If setting SACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION or SCOPE_SECURITY_INFORMATION, the caller must have the SE_SECURITY_NAME privilege enabled. This parameter can be NULL if you are not setting the SACL.
L72: ## Return value
L73: 
L74: If the function succeeds, the function returns ERROR_SUCCESS.
L75: 
L76: If the function fails, it returns a nonzero error code defined in WinError.h.
L77: ## Remarks
L78: 
L79: If you are setting the 【9†discretionary access control list】 (DACL) or any elements in the 【5†system access control list】 (SACL) of an object, the system automatically propagates any inheritable 【10†access control entries】 (ACEs) to existing child objects, according to the 【11†ACE inheritance rules】.
L80: 
L81: You can use the SetSecurityInfo function with the following types of objects:
L82:   * Local or remote files or directories on an NTFS
L83:   * Named pipes
L84:   * Local or remote printers
L85:   * Local or remote Windows services
L86:   * Network shares
L87:   * Registry keys
L88:   * Semaphores, events, mutexes, and waitable timers
L89:   * Processes, threads, jobs, and file-mapping objects
L90:   * Window stations and desktops
L91:   * Directory service objects
L92: The SetSecurityInfo function does not reorder access-allowed or access-denied ACEs based on the preferred order. When propagating inheritable ACEs to existing child objects, SetSecurityInfo puts inherited ACEs in order after all of the noninherited ACEs in the DACLs of the child objects.
L93: Note  If share access to the children of the object is not available, this function will not propagate unprotected ACEs to the children. For example, if a directory is opened with exclusive access, the operating system will not propagate unprotected ACEs to the subdirectories or files of that directory when the security on the directory is changed.
L94: Warning  If the supplied handle was opened with an 【12†ACCESS_MASK】 value of MAXIMUM_ALLOWED, then the SetSecurityInfo function will not propagate ACEs to children.
L95: ## Requirements
L96: 
L97: Requirement  | Value
L98: --- | ---
L99: Minimum supported client  | Windows XP [desktop apps | UWP apps]
L100: Minimum supported server  | Windows Server 2003 [desktop apps | UWP apps]

L24: # SECURITY_INFORMATION
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: The SECURITY_INFORMATION data type identifies the object-related security information being set or queried. This security information includes:
L33: 
L34:   * The owner of an object
L35:   * The primary group of an object
L36:   * The 【5†discretionary access control list】 (DACL) of an object
L37:   * The 【6†system access control list】 (SACL) of an object
L38: 
L39:     `typedef DWORD SECURITY_INFORMATION, *PSECURITY_INFORMATION;
L40:     `
L41: ## Remarks
L42: 
L43: Some SECURITY_INFORMATION members work only with the 【7†SetNamedSecurityInfo】 function. These members are not returned in the structure returned by other security functions such as 【8†GetNamedSecurityInfo】 or 【9†ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptor】.
L44: 
L45: Each item of security information is designated by a bit flag. Each bit flag can be one of the following values. For more information, see the 【10†SetSecurityAccessMask】 and 【11†QuerySecurityAccessMask】 functions.
L46: Value/rights required to query/set  | Meaning
L47: --- | ---
L48: ATTRIBUTE_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L49: Right required to query: READ_CONTROL
L50: Right required to set: WRITE_DAC
L51:  | The resource properties of the object being referenced. The resource properties are stored in SYSTEM_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTE_ACE types in the SACL of the security descriptor.
L52: Windows Server 2008 R2, Windows 7, Windows Server 2008, Windows Vista, Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: This bit flag is not available.
L53: BACKUP_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L54: Right required to query: READ_CONTROL and ACCESS_SYSTEM_SECURITY
L55: Right required to set: WRITE_DAC and WRITE_OWNER and ACCESS_SYSTEM_SECURITY
L56:  | All parts of the security descriptor. This is useful for backup and restore software that needs to preserve the entire security descriptor.
L57: Windows Server 2008 R2, Windows 7, Windows Server 2008, Windows Vista, Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: This bit flag is not available.
L58: DACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L59: Right required to query: READ_CONTROL
L60: Right required to set: WRITE_DAC
L61:  | The DACL of the object is being referenced.
L62: GROUP_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L63: Right required to query: READ_CONTROL
L64: Right required to set: WRITE_OWNER
L65:  | The primary group identifier of the object is being referenced.
L66: LABEL_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L67: Right required to query: READ_CONTROL
L68: Right required to set: WRITE_OWNER
L69:  | The mandatory integrity label is being referenced.
L70: The mandatory integrity label is an ACE in the SACL of the object.
L71: Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: This bit flag is not available.
L72: OWNER_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L73: Right required to query: READ_CONTROL
L74: Right required to set: WRITE_OWNER
L75:  | The owner identifier of the object is being referenced.
L76: PROTECTED_DACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L77: Right required to query: Not available
L78: Right required to set: WRITE_DAC
L79:  | The DACL cannot inherit 【12†access control entries】 (ACEs).
L80: PROTECTED_SACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L81: Right required to query: Not available
L82: Right required to set: ACCESS_SYSTEM_SECURITY
L83:  | The SACL cannot inherit ACEs.
L84: SACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L85: Right required to query: ACCESS_SYSTEM_SECURITY
L86: Right required to set: ACCESS_SYSTEM_SECURITY
L87:  | The SACL of the object is being referenced.
L88: SCOPE_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L89: Right required to query: READ_CONTROL
L90: Right required to set: ACCESS_SYSTEM_SECURITY
L91:  | The Central Access Policy (CAP) identifier applicable on the object that is being referenced. Each CAP identifier is stored in a SYSTEM_SCOPED_POLICY_ID_ACE type in the SACL of the SD.
L92: Windows Server 2008 R2, Windows 7, Windows Server 2008, Windows Vista, Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: This bit flag is not available.
L93: UNPROTECTED_DACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION
L94: Right required to query: Not available
L95: Right required to set: WRITE_DAC
L96:  | The DACL inherits ACEs from the parent object.

L98: Right required to query: Not available
